intro: Cabeza del Buey is a town in Extremadura's Badajoz province, and its tree is really seven trees, growing together in the grounds of a pilgrimage sanctuary eleven kilometres out of town. Dutch elm disease wiped out most of Spain's elms in the twentieth century; this grove survived. Spain named it Tree of the Year in 2017 and it placed second in the European contest the year after, with over 22,000 votes.
meta_description: The Centenary Elms of the Ermita de Belen near Cabeza del Buey: seven old elms that survived Dutch elm disease, Spain's Tree of the Year 2017.
question_meta: Cabeza del Buey's notable tree is the grove of Centenary Elms at the Ermita de Belen. Their age, why they survived, and how to reach them.
question_answer: The trees at Cabeza del Buey are the Centenary Elms of the Ermita de Belen, a group of seven common elms growing together in the grounds of a pilgrimage sanctuary 11 kilometres from town. They are among the few living elm groves in Spain to have survived Dutch elm disease, and Spain named them its Tree of the Year in 2017.
question_context: Three sources describe the same thing: a compact stand of seven Ulmus minor elms in the courtyard of the Santuario de Nuestra Senora de Belen, one grove around a single sanctuary rather than a scattered population. The municipal site calls them los siete olmos centenarios; a travel blog describes them as a cohesive group under a good canopy. Dutch elm disease killed most of Spain's elms through the twentieth century, and Wikipedia and the municipal site both call this one of the few living groves to survive it, though some trunks are hollowed by past damage and the grove has been cordoned and propped to keep it standing. The Junta de Extremadura declared it an Arbol Singular under Decreto 140/2005. It won Spain's national Tree of the Year award in 2017 and placed second in Europe in 2018 with 22,323 votes. Only one height figure is published, 14 metres for a single specimen; no girth has been found for any of the seven. The sanctuary has hosted an annual pilgrimage every 27 September since at least the 17th century, and the grounds sit open beside the public EX-104 road with no gate or charge mentioned anywhere.

faq.q: Where exactly are the Centenary Elms?
faq.a: In the grounds of the Santuario de Nuestra Senora de Belen, on the EX-104 road about 11 kilometres from Cabeza del Buey and 3 kilometres from Almorchon, in Badajoz province.

faq.q: How did they survive Dutch elm disease?
faq.a: Nobody has published why this grove in particular made it through while most of Spain's elms did not. Some trunks are hollowed by past disease damage, and the grove has been cordoned and propped to keep standing.
Sources describe them as centenary, over a hundred years old, without a firmer published figure. Published here as a 150 to 250 year band; if you know of a more precise dating, tell us.

Yes, free and open. The sanctuary grounds sit beside the public EX-104 road with no gate or fee mentioned in any source. No public transport is confirmed; the site is a car journey from Cabeza del Buey.

trees.story:
Dutch elm disease took most of Spain's elms through the twentieth century. Seven of them, growing together in the courtyard of a pilgrimage sanctuary in rural Extremadura, did not go.

The Olmos Centenarios stand in the grounds of the Santuario de Nuestra Senora de Belen, 11 kilometres out of Cabeza del Buey on the road toward Almorchon. Wikipedia and the municipal site both describe this grove as one of the few living stands of elms left in Spain to have survived the disease that wiped out the rest. It was not a clean survival: some of the trunks are hollowed by past infection, and the grove has since been cordoned off and propped up to keep it standing.

The sanctuary itself has hosted an annual pilgrimage every 27 September since at least the 1600s, so these trees have stood through centuries of the same gathering under their canopy. In 2017 Spain named them its Tree of the Year, and the following year they placed second in the European contest with 22,323 votes.

One of the seven has a published height of 14 metres; no girth figure exists anywhere for any of them, despite checking the municipal records and two regional tourism sites. That gap stays open. The grounds sit beside the public EX-104 road with no gate or charge mentioned in any source.
trees.why_go: Most of Spain's elms are gone. This is a whole grove of seven that made it through the disease that took the rest, still standing together around a sanctuary that has drawn a pilgrimage every September for over three centuries, and it won the country's Tree of the Year award for it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise the grove by its setting: seven elms clustered under a shared canopy in the sanctuary courtyard, several with hollowed, propped or cordoned trunks from past disease damage. No other tree group stands at the sanctuary.
trees.access: Free, open. The elms stand in the grounds of a working pilgrimage sanctuary beside the public EX-104 road; the trees are ringed with protective wooden railings to keep visitors off the roots, but the grounds themselves are open with no gate or admission charge mentioned anywhere.
trees.transport: Rural, off the EX-104 road, 11 km from Cabeza del Buey and 3 km from Almorchon; no public transport confirmed, reachable by car.
